about: Numbers the campaign engine uses, each tagged SOURCED, ESTIMATED (with its source and spread) or TUNABLE (with the spread it's checked against). Read by src/core2/campaign-views.ts and src/core2/modules/campaigns.ts.

leanPerDutyBound.source: Gerber, Huber, Doherty, Dowling and Ha (2010), 'Personality and Political Attitudes', American Political Science Review 104(1): conscientiousness predicts conservative self-placement (standardized effects about 0.1 to 0.2).

personalityLeanCorrelation.source: How much of where a person stands left or right their personality accounts for, as a correlation: the rest comes from upbringing, family and life. A meta-analysis of 232 samples (N = 575,691) found openness correlates with conservatism at r = -0.145 and conscientiousness at r = 0.076, the two largest Big Five links (Osborne, Satherley and Sibley 2023, University of Auckland ResearchSpace 2292/56390); a German panel replication found r = -0.07 and 0.06 (Krieger et al. 2019, 'Big-Five Personality and Political Orientation: Results from Four Panel Studies with Representative German Samples', DIW Berlin). Combined, the Big Five predict ideology at a multiple correlation near 0.2 in the United States (Gerber, Huber, Doherty, Dowling and Ha 2010, American Political Science Review 104(1)).

householdLeanShare.source: Share of a person's opening lean, beyond their personality, that their household holds in common, as in PEOPLE's views engine: parent-child correlations of political orientation run about 0.4 to 0.6 (Jennings, Stoker and Bowers 2009, Journal of Politics 71(3):782-799), and spouses correlate about 0.6 on ideology (Alford, Hatemi, Hibbing, Martin and Eaves 2011, Journal of Politics 73(2):362-379).

leanPerGenerous.source: Gerber et al. (2010): agreeableness predicts liberal economic attitudes (effects about -0.05 to -0.15).

leanPerPractical.source: Gerber et al. (2010): openness to experience predicts liberal self-placement; a practical, conventional facet is its low pole (effects about 0.05 to 0.25).

doorsPerCanvasserHour.source: Green and Gerber, Get Out the Vote (4th ed., 2019), ch. 3: canvassers typically reach 12 to 20 doors an hour in residential neighborhoods.

rapportWeight.source: How much a pleasant or awkward meeting itself moves a voter's warmth, beside agreement on the platform. Checked against field-experiment persuasion effects (Kalla and Broockman 2018: near zero on average in general elections, larger in low-information local races).

secondhandWeight.source: Share of a first-hand impression that a retelling passes on to family and friends. Checked against two-step-flow findings (Katz and Lazarsfeld 1955; Nickerson 2008: 60% of a canvassing turnout effect passed to housemates).

donationShareOfCashPerWarmth.source: Share of a supporter's cash on hand they give per unit of warmth, before the legal limit. Checked against typical small-donor gifts (FEC: most individual contributions under $200).

adContactsPerThousandMinor.source: Ten people reached per $10 of ad spending: digital and local broadcast cost per thousand impressions of about $10 to $30 (eMarketer 2024; AdImpact 2024 political CPMs), counting one person reached per several impressions.

adWarmthWeight.source: Share of a first-hand agreement effect an ad carries. Checked against Kalla and Broockman (2018): ad persuasion is small and fades.

doorContactWeight.source: How far one conversation at the door moves a voter toward what they make of the candidate. Checked against field experiments: face-to-face contact is the strongest campaign contact (Green and Gerber 2019).

speechWeight.source: How far hearing a speech moves a listener, below a personal conversation (Green and Gerber 2019 rank events below door contact).

endorsementWeight.source: How far hearing that someone you know endorses a candidate moves you. Checked against endorsement-cue studies (Lupia 1994).

canvasserReliabilityEfficiency.source: Extra (or fewer) doors per hour for each step of a canvasser's reliability.

rivalHoursWithJob.source: Hours a working candidate spends knocking doors on a campaign day: an evening (Green and Gerber 2019 describe volunteer shifts of two to three hours).

rivalHoursWithoutJob.source: Hours a candidate without a job spends knocking doors on a campaign day: two shifts.

minimumVolunteerAge.source: Common campaign practice of taking volunteers from about 16; no single law sets it.

votingStandAgainBase.source: The reason a serving incumbent who is a full person carries to stand again before their traits weigh in (the trait lean for stand over retire runs about -1 to 1, so most incumbents still stand). Checked against the share of incumbents who seek reelection, about 81% of U.S. local incumbents, the figure the repo's candidacy test cites.

turnoutBase.source: The reason to vote every adult carries before their own duty and reliability (on the trait scale, about -4.5 to 4.5), the trait lean between voting and staying home (traitDecisionWeight times about -1 to 1), their interest in the race and its cost. Checked so named adults in a local race on a presidential November turn out near 64% (63.9% of the voting-eligible population voted in November 2024, U.S. Elections Project, Michael McDonald); measured over eight random places and seeds with every trait counted (FIXER-TRAITS-TURNOUT, Oct 13, 2026), 64% at this value.

turnoutWorkWeekMinutes.source: A 40-hour work week in minutes, the unit a voter's weekly work hours are measured against as a cost of getting to the polls (BLS: 40 hours is the standard full-time week).

localElectorateShareOfPopulation.source: Votes cast in November 2024 (about 156 million, Clerk of the House) over the U.S. resident population (about 340 million, Census Bureau Vintage 2024): 0.46. Scaled by each election's cycle (midterm 0.72, off-cycle 0.39 of a presidential year's) where the race's electorate is sized.

voterGroupBands.source: How many lean bands, evenly across the whole left-right scale, the unnamed electorate is split into; each band votes as a group, split the way its named people chose; an even count, so the scale's middle is a band edge and no band spans both sides.

partyIdentifierShare.source: Gallup, party identification 2024 annual average: 28% Democrat and 28% Republican identify with a party (43% independent).

noPartyShare.source: Pew Research Center (2024), 'Changing Partisan Coalitions in a Politically Divided Nation': about 7% of adults neither identify with nor lean toward a party.

partyLoyaltyWeight.source: How much a voter's own party tie adds to its candidate's appeal, beside their lean. Checked against party-line voting: about 95% of party identifiers voted for their party's presidential nominee in 2024 (Pew validated voters).

recordVoteWeight.source: How much each vote on the record moves a voter who knows the officeholder, toward or away by how close the vote sits to their own view. Checked against roll-call accountability studies (Canes-Wrone, Brady and Cogan 2002: members out of step with their districts lose a few points of vote share).

keptPromiseWeight.source: How much a kept promise the voter agreed with adds. Checked against promise-keeping experiments (Bonilla 2022: voters reward kept promises modestly).

brokenPromiseWeight.source: How much a broken promise the voter agreed with takes away; larger than a kept one (negativity bias: Soroka 2014; Bonilla 2022). Checked against pledge experiments with real government pledges (N = 13,000 and 10,000): broken pledges weigh more in voters' evaluations than kept ones (Naurin, Soroka and Markwat 2019, 'Asymmetric Accountability', Comparative Political Studies 52(13-14):2207-2234), and voters care even more that the decision itself matches their own view (Markwat, 'Pledge-based accountability: Voter responses to fulfilled and broken election pledges', doctoral thesis, University of Gothenburg, GUPEA 2077/68335), so a broken promise weighs a little less than the vote that broke it does with a voter who held the promised view (recordVoteWeight times 1.5).

sponsorRelationshipWeight.source: How much a member's relationship with the sponsor (core2 relationship level) adds to their support. Checked against cosponsorship-network studies (Fowler 2006).

dealWeight.source: What one recorded deal (backing their item, a favor) adds to a member's support. Checked against logrolling studies (Stratmann 1992: vote trading moves a few votes on close measures).

constituentWeight.source: How much the district's lean on the questions weighs beside the member's own views. Checked against dyadic representation studies (Miller and Stokes 1963; Bafumi and Herron 2010).

ordinanceEffectiveDays.source: Many city charters and state municipal codes make an ordinance effective 30 days after passage unless it says otherwise or is an emergency (e.g. Cal. Gov. Code 36937; Ohio Rev. Code 731.29 sets 30 days). Varies by place: SG-GOV-veto-override-rule's companion, to be read per state.

appointmentAcquaintanceWeight.source: How much knowing a candidate adds to an appointing official's choice, beside alignment and qualification. Checked against patronage studies (Lewis 2008: personal and campaign ties shape appointments, most of all to lower-profile posts).

identityLeanScale.source: A named official not filled in yet leans this far toward their seat's party: state legislators' ideal points sit well inside their party's side (Shor and McCarty 2011, state legislative ideology: party medians near +/-0.6 to 0.9 of the scale).

committeeOfTheWholeMaximum.source: Councils of up to about nine members usually work as a committee of the whole rather than through standing committees (National League of Cities, city council committee practice; ICMA 2018 survey: median council size 6).

hearingWitnesses.source: How many of the people a bill touches most testify at its hearing; hearings commonly seat a few public witnesses per panel.

budgetAdoptionDuty.source: How much a member's duty to keep the government funded weighs toward adopting a budget, beside their views on its changes. Checked against how rarely councils fail to adopt a budget (most charters carry the prior budget forward when they do).

floorBillsPerLegislativeDay.source: How many bills a legislative chamber's floor takes up in one floor day (each bill reached is debated and voted on; the rest die at adjournment). Checked against official session totals: Kentucky 2024, 212 bills became law in 60 legislative days (3.5 a day, each passing both chambers); Florida 2024, 313 bills passed both chambers in a 60-day session (about 5 a day); the floor also takes up bills that fail (data/research/lawmaking-throughput/throughput-evidence.json).

legislativeDaysPerWeek.source: Floor days a week while a state legislature is in session, applied to the session's recorded length (NCSL 2026 session calendar). Checked against Kentucky 2024: 60 legislative days between January 2 and April 15, about four a week (Kentucky Legislative Research Commission, General Assembly Action: 2024 Regular Session).

congressFloorDaysPerYear.source: Days a year Congress's floor sits to take up bills. Checked against the House calendar's statistical summary: 184 legislative days in 2023, counting pro forma days with no votes (House Calendars, March 1, 2024, 118th Congress, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CCAL-118hcal-2024-03-01/html/CCAL-118hcal-2024-03-01-pt19.htm), and the 118th Congress's 274 public laws in two years (Clerk of the House, final calendar of the 118th Congress).

fullYearSessionAgendaMonth.source: The month at whose end a legislature that sits all year (NCSL 'full-year') brings its leader's priority bills to the floor: the end of the state fiscal year most share (June 30 in 46 states, NASBO), when full-time legislatures pass their headline measures alongside the budget.

congressAgendaDayOfYear.source: The day of the year (349 = December 15) Congress brings its majority leader's priority policy bills to the floor: the final scheduled voting weeks of the House calendar, when year-end packages pass (House majority leader's 2025 and 2026 calendars).

senateClotureShare.source: U.S. Senate Standing Rules, Rule XXII(2): debate on a measure ends only when three-fifths of the senators duly chosen and sworn vote for cloture; the bill then passes by a majority of those voting. https://www.rules.senate.gov/rules-of-the-senate

localRegularMeetingsPerYear.source: Regular meetings a year of a town council or county board, each with legislation on its agenda: most councils meet once or twice a month (National League of Cities, City Councils in the U.S., 2023).

localMeetingAgendaMinutes.source: Minutes of a regular council or board meeting given to legislation, after consent items and reports (regular meetings commonly run two to four hours; National League of Cities, City Councils in the U.S., 2023).

policyOrdinanceMinutes.source: Minutes one policy ordinance takes on a meeting's agenda: its staff report, public comment and the members' debate and vote. Checked against Minneapolis 2024: 48 ordinances introduced and 47 enacted over the year, besides 449 resolutions (Minneapolis City Council tracking report, data/research/lawmaking-throughput/throughput-evidence.json).

defeatedMeasureWaitDays.source: Days after a council or board votes a measure down before the same measure may come back: Robert's Rules of Order (12th ed., 38:1) lets a defeated motion be renewed only at a later session, and council rules of procedure commonly bar a defeated ordinance for six months to a year.

recallOrganizerEffort.source: How strongly a resident must be moved (their grievance with a member's vote plus the weighted trait lean between organizing and leaving it, about -1 to 1 on the shared trait scale, recalls.organize) before taking on a recall petition drive. Checked against local recall frequency: Ballotpedia counts about 150 to 250 local recall efforts a year across roughly 90,000 local governments.

recallElectionDays.source: Days from a recall petition's certification to the recall vote (state laws commonly set 60 to 90 days, or the next regular election).

recallThresholdEstimate.source: Percent of the votes last cast for the office that a local recall petition needs where the state's recall exists but its threshold isn't read: the median of the read municipal recall rules (25%, Colorado, Michigan, Arizona, New Jersey; 15% Oregon).

groupDuesMinor.source: A year's dues for a small business in a local employers' association, in cents: local chambers of commerce charge small firms about $300 to $700 a year (chamber dues schedules surveyed by the U.S. Chamber's local affiliate guides).

groupJoinBar.source: How strongly a resident must feel about a bill's question (stances run about 0 to 0.7, doubled where it touches their own life), with their trait lean toward joining added (about -1 to 1 times the trait weight), to join a group over it: checked over two random played worlds so a small share join on the most divisive questions and almost none on mild ones, near the roughly one in ten adults who report working with others in their community to solve a problem in a year (AmeriCorps and Census Bureau, Civic Engagement and Volunteering Supplement, 2021 to 2023).

groupFoundingMembers.source: How many residents must join before a group exists: an association needs a handful of founders to hold office (state nonprofit corporation acts commonly require three directors or incorporators).

lobbyWeight.source: How much a member a group met weighs its case, at full strength when the group speaks for all of the bill's losers; checked so a fully organized industry moves a member about as much as their constituents' lean does.

executivePriorityShare.source: The largest share of a budget line an executive's proposal moves it in a year, at full lean on a line the parties split on completely; checked against year-over-year changes in proposed functional spending (presidential and gubernatorial budget requests typically move a function a few percent).

officeHoursPerMonth.source: How often a local official's office holds open hours where residents bring problems (many council members hold monthly office hours or a monthly ward meeting).

caseEffort.source: How much a problem must press on a resident, plus their readiness to reach out, before they bring it to an official; checked so a small share of residents with a problem come in a given month (about 1 in 5 Americans contacted an elected official in the past year: Pew, 2018).

constituentHelpBase.source: How readily an official with no staffer helps a resident's case before their traits tilt it (scaled trait lean runs about -1 to 1): most do, and only strongly unhelpful temperaments turn one away (OPUS-TRAITS, Oct 12, 2026).

caseRetirementAge.source: Earliest age for Social Security retirement benefits (SSA); an adult past it without work isn't read as looking for work.

caseCushionMonths.source: Months of savings against living costs below which being out of work presses hard (the common three-month emergency-fund guideline; Federal Reserve SHED 2024: 63% could cover a $400 expense from cash).

caseResponseDays.source: Days before an office handles a case the official hasn't decided themselves.

caseHelpedWarmth.source: Where a resident's view of an official heads after being helped (or the opposite after being turned away).

caseWeight.source: How far one case moves a resident's view toward that, at full severity.

caseWageShortfallScale.source: How hard being paid under the minimum wage presses: the shortfall's share of the legal wage times this (a 20% shortfall presses fully).

staffHourlyMinor.source: A local official's aide's pay, in cents an hour: legislative assistants earn about $45,000 to $55,000 a year (BLS OES 2024, 43-6011 executive secretaries and administrative assistants in local government, median about $24 an hour).

staffReviewDays.source: Days between an official's looks at whether their office needs a hand: hiring for a public post runs on a weeks-long cycle (posting, interviews, start).

staffPerOfficial.source: Personal staff an official with a seat takes on: local elected officials commonly have one aide or share clerical staff (National League of Cities, City Councils in the U.S., 2023: most council members in small and mid-size cities have no or shared staff; mayors and county officers have an assistant), state legislators one to three (NCSL, Size of State Legislative Staff, 2015).

staffHireBase.source: How readily an official takes on the aide their office allows before their trait lean toward hiring over doing it alone (scaled trait lean runs about -1 to 1): most do, the most self-reliant don't.

staffKnownWeight.source: How much knowing a candidate adds to an official's choice of aide beside how well they'd do the work: officials hire through their own networks first (Congressional Management Foundation, 'Life in Congress: The Member Perspective', 2013; most staff come through campaign and personal contacts).

staffBaseQuality.source: Where a new staffer's work starts before their reliability, deliberation, experience and passion add or take away.

staffLearningBase.source: How fast experience grows per task done, before a staffer's own deliberation speeds or slows it.

staffExperienceCeiling.source: The most experience adds to a staffer's work.

staffPassionWeight.source: How much caring about a task's question adds to a staffer's work on it.

staffCaseFollowThrough.source: How good a staffer's work on a case must be for them to see it through to a referral.

staffTraitWeight.source: How much each of a staffer's reliability and deliberation (each from -1 to 1) moves their work.

caseRepeatDays.source: How long after bringing a problem to an official a resident waits before bringing one again.

midtermSwing.source: How far the president's party's two-party House share falls in a midterm: about 2 to 3 points on average since 1946 (the president's party lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms; Gallup and the Brookings Vital Statistics on Congress).

incumbencyShare.source: The two-party vote share an incumbent's party gains from holding the seat: about 2 to 3 points in recent House elections, down from 6 to 8 in the 1980s (Jacobson, The Politics of Congressional Elections, 2020 edition).

legislativeSeatMargin.source: How far a state legislative district without a read result leans to its holder's party, in two-party share: the median state legislative general election margin is about 25 points (Ballotpedia, 'Margin of victory analysis for the 2024 state legislative elections'), so about 0.12 of share.

primaryTurnoutCost.source: What a primary adds to the cost of voting, against a general election: checked so a party's primary turnout lands near the real 20 to 30% of its eligible voters (Bipartisan Policy Center, 2022 primary turnout: about 21% of registered voters; Pew 2022). Measured over eight random places and seeds with every trait counted (FIXER-TRAITS-TURNOUT, Oct 13, 2026): 25 to 34% of named adults clear this cost.

primaryShareOfGeneral.source: Primary voters as a share of the same year's general-election voters: 2022 statewide primaries cast about 21% of registered voters' ballots against about 46% in November (Bipartisan Policy Center and U.S. Elections Project), so about 0.45.

partyMeetingDays.source: Days between a local party committee's meetings: county and town committees commonly meet monthly under their party rules (e.g. state party bylaws for county committees), some every other month or quarterly.

partyMeetingAttendBar.source: How far a member's trait lean toward attending (about -1 to 1) must reach for them to show up at a party meeting: only the most inclined do, checked against the 6 to 10% of adults who report attending a political meeting in a year (American National Election Studies, 'attended political meetings', 2016 to 2024).

partiesJoinBase.source: Most people tied to a party affiliate (Pew Research Center party-identification surveys: about two thirds of adults identify with or lean toward a party); the trait lean toward joining (about -1 to 1) is added, so only the most reluctant stay out.

incumbentRecognition.source: How much an incumbent's name on the ballot draws a voter no campaign reached (ballot recognition; incumbents win about 98% of House primaries, Ballotpedia 2024).

midtermShareOfPresidential.source: Turnout in the 2022 midterm (46.6% of the voting-eligible population) over 2024's presidential turnout (64.1%): 0.72 (U.S. Elections Project, Michael McDonald).

offCycleShareOfPresidential.source: Off-cycle city election turnout against a presidential year's: big-city mayoral turnout runs about 0.39 of presidential turnout off cycle, 0.72 on midterm dates and 0.91 on presidential dates (Hajnal and Green, 'Big Cities, Tiny Votes?', Dec 2024; FIXER stand-in figures, Oct 12, SG-GOV-voter-groups-stand-in).

midtermTurnoutCost.source: What a midterm adds to the cost of voting against a presidential year (less attention and interest), checked so named turnout falls near the 2022 midterm's 46.6% of the voting-eligible population (U.S. Elections Project, Michael McDonald), 0.72 of a presidential year's; measured over eight random places and seeds with every trait counted (FIXER-TRAITS-TURNOUT, Oct 13, 2026), 46% at this value.

offCycleTurnoutCost.source: What an off-cycle election adds to the cost of voting, checked so named turnout falls near 0.39 of a presidential year's, about 25% of eligible adults (Hajnal and Green, 'Big Cities, Tiny Votes?', 2024; off-cycle mayoral turnout in large cities averages about 20% of eligible voters, Portland State University, 'Who Votes for Mayor?', 2016); measured over eight random places and seeds with every trait counted (FIXER-TRAITS-TURNOUT, Oct 13, 2026), 25 to 34% at this value.

officeTermYearsEstimate.source: The term of a local or county office whose own term isn't read: most county and municipal elected offices serve four-year terms (National Association of Counties, County Structure and Elected Officials; ICMA Municipal Form of Government Survey 2023).

votedShareOfRegistered.source: Share of registered voters who voted in November 2024: 65.3% of citizens voted and 73.6% were registered (U.S. Census Bureau, Voting and Registration in the Election of November 2024, CPS), so about 0.89.

tieElectionDays.source: Days from a tied election to the second election between the tied candidates, where the law calls for one: states set special or runoff elections three to six weeks out (e.g. Georgia runoffs four weeks after the general).

canvassStartHour.source: When a canvassing shift starts: early evening, when most people are home (Green and Gerber, Get Out the Vote, 2019: weekday evening and weekend canvassing).

doorAnswerThreshold.source: How ready the adult home whose traits lean most toward opening must be to open to a canvasser (every trait's lean between opening and ignoring, campaigns.open-door, times traitScale, about -3 to 3, plus their age term); checked against field contact rates of about a quarter to a third of doors knocked (Green and Gerber, Get Out the Vote, 2019; Arceneaux 2005). Measured over six random places and seeds with every trait counted (FIXER-TRAITS-TURNOUT, Oct 13, 2026): 19 to 37% of doors, 31% on average, at this value; 42 to 61% at the earlier 1.25.

volunteerClosenessWeight.source: How much closeness to the candidate (relationship level, family) weighs in agreeing to volunteer.

volunteerThreshold.source: How strong someone's pull to volunteer must be (their warmth and closeness to the candidate, every trait's lean between volunteering and declining, campaigns.volunteer, times traitScale, about -3 to 3, less their hours of work): checked so a small share of a candidate's acquaintances say yes (about 4% of adults worked or volunteered for a campaign in 2020, ANES; a candidate's friends and family volunteer at several times that). Measured over six random places and seeds with every trait counted (FIXER-TRAITS-TURNOUT, Oct 13, 2026): 5 to 31% of acquaintances, 17% on average, at this value; 21 to 54% at the earlier 1.0.

doorAnswerPivotAge.source: The age around which answering a canvasser's knock neither rises nor falls in a person's readiness.

doorAnswerAgeSpan.source: Years of age that move readiness to answer by one step (older residents answer more; Green and Gerber 2019).

pollCostPerInterviewMinor.source: What a campaign pays per completed telephone interview: $36 to $53 (midpoint about $45; BMC Medical Research Methodology 12:32), $46 to $80 by web; a whole local poll of a few hundred interviews runs $15,000 to $40,000 (Daily Montanan, 2023), consistent. data/research/money/poll-interview-prices.json (carried from #2486). Not scaled by place.

pollAnswerThreshold.source: How ready (sociability, half their reliability, and age) someone called must be to complete a poll; checked against telephone response rates of about 6 to 10% (Pew Research Center 2019).

pollPartyCue.source: How firm a lean must be for someone no campaign reached to name their party's candidate to a pollster rather than say they're undecided.

committeeSize.source: State legislative standing committees hold about 10 to 12 members whatever the chamber's size (Book of the States 2023, Table 3.23; Ballotpedia's 2021 count of 2,083 state legislative committees; NCSL chamber sizes, June 2024).

committeeSizeMinimum.source: Smallest common standing committee (Ballotpedia 2021 committee-size breakdown).

committeeSizeMaximum.source: Largest common standing committee (Ballotpedia 2021 committee-size breakdown).

vetoOverrideShare.source: Two thirds is the modal override rule, counted against all members of the body rather than those voting (New York City Charter: 34 of 51; Iowa Code 380.6(2); U.S. Const. art. I, sec. 7 counts each house present). FIXER stand-in figures, Oct 12, SG-GOV-veto-override-rule.

leadershipSeniorityWeight.source: Seniority counts only slightly in choosing leaders and committee members in every chamber type (data/research/legislature/chamber-leadership.json: seniorityImportance 'slight' for all, from NCSL, House and Senate rules and NLC): about a twentieth of a party-line difference per year served.

appointmentExperienceWeight.source: How much working in the department already adds to a resident's qualification for heading it (department heads are usually promoted from within or hired from the field: ICMA local government management surveys).

appointmentBaseQualification.source: What an adult resident with no years of experience, no work in the department and a neutral temperament brings to heading it; with the age term it puts a typical 35-year-old near one half, the old fixed starting score. Checked against the share of appointees who are long-serving residents of the town (ICMA local government management surveys).

appointmentTemperamentWeight.source: How much a resident's reliability and deliberation (summed, each on a -1 to 1 scale) add to or take from their qualification for a department: conscientiousness is the personality trait that best predicts job performance across occupations (Barrick and Mount 1991, Personnel Psychology 44).

appointmentAdulthoodAge.source: Age of majority in 46 states (19 in Alabama and Nebraska, 21 in Mississippi); the game uses the common 18 as the first year of adult working experience, matching the working-age minimum used in town employment (canonical town-employment.ts WORKING_AGE_MIN=18). Structural: below it nobody holds a post.

appointmentExperienceHalfYears.source: Years of adult life at which experience counts half of its full weight toward heading a department; the median age of local department heads is in the low-to-mid 40s, about 25 years past adulthood, and public-sector median tenure with an employer is about 6.5 years (BLS Employee Tenure, 2024; ICMA Municipal Year Book).

appointmentExperienceAgeWeight.source: The most that years of adult experience can add to a resident's qualification, approached smoothly with age and never switched on at an age (department heads are seldom the youngest adults but are not barred from it).

cabinetQualificationBase.source: Qualification of the most qualified of a governor's cabinet candidates, who come from the governor's circle of experienced officials (National Governors Association, Cabinet Appointments in the States).

cabinetQualificationStep.source: How much less qualified each later candidate in a governor's cabinet shortlist is than the one before.

cabinetLeanSpread.source: Share of the governor-side lean each later cabinet candidate gives up: governors draw shortlists from their own coalition but not all of it sits at the governor's own position (NGA cabinet appointment surveys).

confirmationTolerance.source: How far (on the -1 to 1 lean scale) a nominee's views may sit from a member's before the member votes to reject: confirming bodies defer to executives; the U.S. Senate has rejected only nine cabinet nominees in its history (Senate Historical Office), and state senates rarely reject a governor's.

executiveReviewDays.source: Days between an executive's reviews of vacant posts and the orders their office may give: a mayor's or governor's office acts on a vacancy within weeks (city charters commonly have the mayor fill a department head's vacancy promptly, with an acting head meanwhile).

appointeeHourlyMinor.source: Hourly pay of an appointed town department head: BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2023, local government excluding schools and hospitals (OEWS designation), management occupations (11-0000), median hourly wage about $46. Small towns pay less and large cities more.

specialFilingDaysBefore.source: Days before a special election its filing closes where the place's own deadline isn't read; state special-election calendars commonly close filing six to eight weeks ahead.

turnoutEngagementWeight.source: How much following politics closely (PEOPLE's views engine, CES 2024 news interest, 0 to 1) adds to a person's reason to vote, against the national average. Checked against turnout by age: in the 2022 midterm about 23% of citizens 18 to 24 voted and about 65% of those 65 and over (U.S. Census Bureau, CPS Voting and Registration Supplement 2022).

ballotRelationshipWeight.source: How much a voter's own relationship with a candidate they know personally (-1 to 1) adds to that candidate's appeal, beside views and party. Personal contact with a candidate raises support in local races (Gerber and Green 2000, American Political Science Review 94(3):653-663, on face-to-face contact; Arceneaux and Nickerson 2009 on local candidate canvassing). PW-3.

countedRecognitionWeight.source: What being known in town adds to a candidate's appeal for a counted voter no campaign reached, times the share of the town's named adults who have heard of the candidate. Name recognition is the main cue in low-information local races (Ballotpedia 2024 local election analyses; Kam and Zechmeister 2013, 'Name Recognition and Candidate Support', American Journal of Political Science 57(4):971-986). Set above incumbentRecognition (0.15) so a candidate the whole town knows outdraws a bare incumbent's name. PW-3.

votingBallotAgainstViewMax.source: How far a named voter's ballot may run against their own recorded view (the views engine's lean over its maximum, 0 to 1) before it must carry a recorded reason that outweighs the view: 0.5 is the views engine's 'liberal' or 'conservative' label (lean ±1 of ±2). Read by the ballot checks (PW-3); the ballot itself weighs the view, never this number.
